# quick :: rv_corn_wheat

**Q:** With corn's balance sheet where it is, what does that do to wheat on the feed side, and how do the two sheets compare this marketing year?

**TL;DR.** Corn's US sheet is the tight one and wheat's is the loose one: corn's stocks-to-use sits at 0.121393 ratio for MY2026 [N27], down from 0.14499 in MY2025 [N28], while soft red winter wheat's stocks-to-use reads 0.652178 [N34]. That combination points toward higher corn prices via a thin buffer, and it is the one channel that supports the wheat board too -- expensive corn pulls feed wheat into rations -- but the wheat balance sheet itself, plus a spring wheat area reading at the 1st percentile of its own record [N42], leaves wheat the follower, not the leader.

**Why.** ## Mechanism
Take the axes one at a time.

- **Balance-sheet tightness.** Corn's carryout buffer is the binding one; wheat's is not. A tight stocks-to-use ratio is the classic convexity: the model signs higher stocks-to-use as price-pressuring and tight ratios as price-lifting, so a supply shock into corn's thin buffer is right-tailed while the same shock into wheat's cushion is close to linear.
- **Dominant driver.** On corn the loud, high-confidence rows lean opposite ways -- a tight stocks-to-use ratio and high feed demand point up, a large planted area points down. On soft red winter wheat, harvested area is the furthest-from-history reading and, signed opposite on price, is the one genuinely price-supportive structural leg.
- **Shared macro.** Both markets read the same tropical Pacific series under two names; the model gives it opposite signs on each board by phase, so it is one source of risk, not two, and its stated effect window has already closed. Both also carry the same nitrogen-cost channel, currently soft and thus not supportive.
- **The linkage itself.** The model carries the feed-ration substitution both ways: cheap feed wheat displaces corn demand, and higher corn prices pull feed wheat demand and lift the wheat-corn spread floor. That is the transmission -- corn tightness supports wheat through the ration, and the record documents that switch happening in both directions [E1][E2][E4].

## The record
- Corn stocks-to-use 0.121393 ratio for MY2026 [N27] versus 0.14499 for MY2025 [N28] -- a tightening, and read as of 2026-09-11.
- Soft red winter wheat stocks-to-use 0.652178 ratio for MY2026 [N34], on its own marketing year; the two ratios are dimensionless and comparable, the tonnage levels are not.
- Corn feed use 154,947 (1000 MT) for MY2026 [N29] against 161,297 (1000 MT) for MY2025 [N30] -- lower year on year; soft red winter wheat feed use 2,177 (1000 MT) for MY2026 [N31] against 3,244 (1000 MT) for MY2025 [N35], also lower. Both feed channels contracted, so the ration is not currently switching toward wheat on the measured record.
- Corn planted area 35.82 M ha for 2026 [N67], at the 98th percentile of its own record [N69] -- the price-pressuring leg against the tight ratio.
- Soft red winter wheat harvested area 12.97 M ha for 2026 [N40], -2.5 sigma [N41] and the 1st percentile of its own record [N42].
- Direction the record documents: US corn season-average farm price rose from $3.56/bu in MY2019/20 [N103] to $4.53/bu in MY2020/21 [N104] -- a settled USDA survey actual, not a futures settle and not a forecast.
- Corn feed substitution is documented in both directions: corn displaced feed wheat in MY2021/22 when corn was the cheaper ingredient (reported 2021-10-14) [E1]; feed wheat was expected to stay cheaper than corn in MY2018/19 (reported 2018-03-15) [E2]; and USDA cut corn feed and residual use on better soft red winter wheat production prospects (reported 2011-04-08) [E4]. US wheat ending stocks were reported higher in April 2024 [E10].
- Coverage gaps, stated plainly: several stocks-to-use and feed-use lookups returned no rows at all at this as-of -- the record carries no figure for those scopes, not a zero. No front delivery month could be named on either board this session, so there is no price tape behind this page.
- Recency, by layer: the number rows are read as of 2026-09-16, with the newest knowledge date 20260904 and the oldest 2026-08-12; the newest dated document behind this answer is 2024-04-24; the board price tape is not carried on this page.

## Where the record disagrees
Corn's own high-confidence rows point opposite ways and neither dominates on confidence alone. planted area at the 98th percentile [N69] points toward lower. I lean to the tightness leg dominating, because the carryout ratio is where the convexity lives -- a large acreage number is already inside that ratio, while a shock is not. Two of the eight drivers of the price-pressuring big-crop pattern sit among the largest moves here, short of that pattern's own three-driver threshold, so conditions are consistent with it but incomplete.

Separately, the wheat feed-demand story and the wheat balance sheet disagree: the substitution channel says corn tightness supports wheat, while measured wheat feed use fell year on year [N31] versus 3,244 (1000 MT) [N35] and stocks-to-use sits high [N34]. The ration channel is real but it is not currently the largest move on the wheat sheet.

## What to watch
- **The tropical Pacific reading on corn** [N43]: +1.8 degC in July 2026, +2.4 sigma [N44], eight straight months rising and past the strong line. The model signs the warm phase as price-pressuring for corn via favourable Midwest rains, at medium confidence, so a continued run argues against the tight-carryout leg. Conditional on the declared lag counted from that reading's date, the effect window would run 2026-10-31 to 2027-04-30. It reads wrong if the next print turns back inside that line or the run breaks.
- **Soft red winter wheat area** [N40]: 12.97 M ha, bottom decile of its own record, signed opposite on price and therefore the wheat board's own supportive leg. It reads wrong if the next print returns the series to the middle of its own record.
- **Nitrogen cost on wheat** [N73]: -0.53 z for 2026M09, four straight months falling and not across the elevated line; the model signs urea cost as price-supportive with a one-to-three-quarter lag, so a falling reading withholds that support. Conditional on the declared lag counted from that reading's date, the window would run 2026-11-01 to 2027-05-01. It reads wrong if the run breaks before the line.

Nothing else cleared the bar; the US cattle herd at the 1st percentile of its own record [N63] is the alternate I would take next, on the model's four-to-eight-quarter forward feed-demand channel.

**Cascade / convergence**
